posts.text:
Is the US homeownership rate 65%?
Or is it actually 53%?

The Minneapolis Fed just released important research that rethinks our understanding of the US homeownership rate.

The US Census rate of 65% measures the percent of homes that are OWNER OCCUPIED. 
That metric doesn't work well in this era where adult children increasingly live with their parents.

The Minneapolis Fed looks at what % of the adult population owns a home. "HPOP"
That number is much lower -- only 53%.

Important read: minnea

posts.text:
Here's the (good) surprise in the June inflation report: Many items saw a decline in prices.

It was more than falling gas prices.
Electricity was down a bit
Car costs were down a bit
Apparel costs were down a bit
Transportation costs were down a bit
Even medical service costs were down a bit (!)

 This is why Core Inflation was flat in June and cooled to 2.6% in the past year (down from 2.9% in May).

It's still tough for middle-class and moderate-income Americans.

Inflation: 3.5% in the past year
Wage gains: 3.5% in the past year

Inflation is wiping out wage gains for many.
Grocery prices also continue to rise.
But the picture did look slightly better in June than in April or May. The decline in gas prices, along with declines in electricity, apparel and medical care help. 

The question is whether this relief is only temporary as the war in Iran restarts...

posts.text:
Why are Americans so frustrated by grocery prices?

It's simple:
A) Prices rose a lot in recent years (over 25% in past 5 yrs)
B) Grocery prices barely moved in the 2014-2019 years. Relatively speaking, the past few years are a BIG shock for Americans.

Good chart from @econJaredB on historical grocery price growth vs. wages.

Worth watching: The prime-age labor force participation rate fell sharply in June.

Prime-age labor force participation rate June: 83.3%
Primage-age labor force participation rate May: 83.9%

As @fcastofthemonth  points out, this one-month decline of -0.6pp is the biggest one-month drop since the series began in 1948 (excluding April 2020)

Normally when you see something this *weird* it turns out to be a statistical quirk that gets reversed the next month. But we'll see...

The big picture: It's a better job market than a year ago, but the opportunities are limited.

2024 jobs added average: 122,000 a month
2025 jobs added average: 10,000 a month --> "hiring recession"
2026 jobs added average (so far): 92,000 a month

Healthcare and social assistance jobs remain the key driver of job growth. Over HALF of the jobs added in 2026 have been from healthcare/social assist.

#jobs

posts.text:
The unemployment rate fell to 4.2%, the lowest in a year.
Normally that's good news, but not this time.

-720,000 people left the labor force. They aren't even looking for jobs anymore.
-507,000 people are no longer employed.

The employment-to-population ratio fell to 59%, the lowest in about 5 years (since Oct. 2021).

JUST IN: A disappointing jobs report. The US economy added 57,000 jobs in June (below expectations of 115k). Hospitality jobs decline by -61k. Plus, April and May were revised lower by -74,000. 

The unemployment rate fell to 4.2% --> the lowest in a year, but mainly due to a big drop in people job hunting.

The bad news = Wages aren’t keeping up with inflation. Wage gains were 3.5% in the past year, which is below ~4% inflation.

posts.text:
Encouraging news: Job openings are at the highest level in 2 years.

May 2026: 7.6 million job openings
May 2025: 7.3 million job openings
May 2024: 7.8 million job openings

Industries with more job opening than a year ago:
+Most blue collar industries (manufacturing, construction, mining)
+Retail
+Professional and business services

Industries with fewer job openings than a year ago:
-Tech (information)
-Finance/insurance
-Healthcare
-Hospitality
